question:
This is the CLRS chip-testing problem, asked in the D. E. Shaw Hiring Manager round (the candidate proposed O(n^2) and was expected to do better).

You have n chips, and **more than half are good**. Any two chips can be tested against each other: each chip reports whether the other is good or bad. A good chip always reports correctly; a bad chip may report anything. Using only these pairwise tests, **find one good chip using fewer than O(n^2) tests.**
lookingFor: Careful case analysis of what a pairwise test reveals
Finding an invariant (good chips stay a strict majority) that supports a recursion
Moving from a brute-force O(n^2) idea to an O(n) or O(n log n) divide-and-conquer
Handling odd n and proving correctness
answer:
**What a test tells you** (reports are A about B, then B about A):
- Both say "good": both are good, or both are bad.
- Anything else (at least one says "bad"): at least one of the two is bad.

So a test never certifies a chip alone, but "at least one bad" lets us throw both chips away without losing the majority.

**Algorithm (pairing and halving):**
1. Pair up the chips and test each pair.
2. If the pair reports "both good", keep **one** chip of the pair. Otherwise discard both.
3. Recurse on the kept chips.

**Invariant:** good chips remain a strict majority.
- Discarded pairs contain at least one bad chip, so each discarded pair has at least as many bad chips as good.
- Kept pairs are both good or both bad, so one kept chip per pair preserves the ratio between good and bad exactly.
- Since good started as a strict majority, removing pairs with good not exceeding bad leaves good a strict majority.

**Odd n:** set one chip x aside and test it against all n-1 others. If at least half of the verdicts say "good", x is good (a bad x would be called bad by every good chip, which is a strict majority of the others), so return x. Otherwise x is bad: discard it, and the remaining even number of chips still has a strict good majority. This costs O(n) at that level.

**Cost:** at most floor(n/2) tests per round and at most about n/2 chips survive, so T(n) is at most T(n/2) + O(n), which solves to **O(n) tests**. When one chip remains, it is good (majority invariant, size 1).

**Bonus:** once you hold a verified-good chip, test it against all others to classify every chip in n-1 more tests.
followUps: Why can't you simply keep both chips when a pair says both good?
What happens if exactly half the chips are good?
How would you handle odd n cleanly and prove the bound?
Can you do it in n/2 tests? What is the lower bound idea?
